```{python}
import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, roc_auc_score, roc_curve,
                             confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay,
                             classification_report)

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
df = pd.read_csv("C:/Users/Alex/Documents/GitHub/Portfolio/Data/YoungAdults.csv")
```

## Background

Binary classification predicts a yes or no outcome. Here we tackle a behavioral question from the Young People Survey, a questionnaire of about 1,000 young adults on their habits, personalities, and lifestyles: can we tell a current smoker apart from someone who has never smoked, using only their demographics, lifestyle, and personality scores?

To keep the contrast clean, we focus on the two clear ends of the spectrum, current smokers versus people who never smoked, and set aside the ambiguous middle groups who tried smoking or used to smoke. This is the machine-learning sibling of my Logistic Regression analysis, but with many mixed-type predictors and a full preprocessing pipeline.

## Preparing the Data

We label current smokers as 1, never-smokers as 0, and assemble a mix of numeric features such as age, weight, and personality scores along with categorical ones such as gender, alcohol use, and education.

```{python}
#| echo: true
df = df.dropna(subset=["Smoking"])
df = df[df["Smoking"].isin(["current smoker", "never smoked"])].copy()
df["target"] = (df["Smoking"] == "current smoker").astype(int)

numeric = ["Age", "Height", "Weight", "Number_of_siblings", "Fear_score",
           "Religiosity_score", "Music_diversity_score", "Happiness_score"]
categorical = ["Gender", "Education", "Only_child", "Alcohol",
               "I_live_a_healthy_lifestyle", "Punctuality", "Lying"]

X, y = df[numeric + categorical], df["target"]
print(f"Current smokers: {(y==1).sum()}   Never smoked: {(y==0).sum()}")
```

The two classes are nicely balanced, so accuracy will be a meaningful metric because no single class dominates.

## Building a Preprocessing Pipeline

Real survey data mixes numbers and text and has gaps. A scikit-learn pipeline with a column transformer handles all of it in one object: numeric features are median-imputed and standardized, while categorical features are mode-imputed and one-hot encoded. Bundling preprocessing with the model prevents information from leaking between the train and test sets.

```{python}
#| echo: true
preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                      ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric),
    ("cat", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
                      ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"))]), categorical),
])

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y)
```

## Training and Comparing Models

We compare a logistic regression against a random forest, both wrapped in the same preprocessing pipeline and both class-balanced.

```{python}
#| echo: true
models = {
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced"),
    "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=42,
                                            n_jobs=1, class_weight="balanced"),
}

rows, fitted = [], {}
for name, clf in models.items():
    pipe = Pipeline([("prep", preprocess), ("clf", clf)]).fit(X_train, y_train)
    fitted[name] = pipe
    proba = pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    rows.append({"Model": name,
                 "Accuracy": round(accuracy_score(y_test, pipe.predict(X_test)), 3),
                 "ROC-AUC": round(roc_auc_score(y_test, proba), 3)})
pd.DataFrame(rows)
```

Both models land around 66% accuracy with a ROC-AUC near 0.72, clearly better than a coin flip. AUC, the probability the model ranks a random smoker above a random non-smoker, is the fairer headline here because it does not depend on a specific threshold.

## The ROC Curve

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
for name, pipe in fitted.items():
    proba = pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, proba)
    ax.plot(fpr, tpr, lw=2, label=f"{name} (AUC={roc_auc_score(y_test, proba):.2f})")
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=1, label="Chance")
ax.set_xlabel("False Positive Rate"); ax.set_ylabel("True Positive Rate")
ax.set_title("ROC Curve for Smoker vs Never-Smoker")
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Confusion Matrix and Report

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
best = fitted["Random Forest"]
pred = best.predict(X_test)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4.5))
ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(
    y_test, pred, ax=ax, cmap="Blues", colorbar=False,
    display_labels=["Never", "Current"])
ax.set_title("Confusion Matrix for the Random Forest")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

```{python}
print(classification_report(y_test, pred, target_names=["Never smoked", "Current smoker"]))
```

## Which Features Matter Most?

Reading importances back through the pipeline shows which survey answers most separate smokers from non-smokers.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
rf = fitted["Random Forest"]
names = rf.named_steps["prep"].get_feature_names_out()
imp = (pd.Series(rf.named_steps["clf"].feature_importances_, index=names)
         .sort_values(ascending=False).head(10).sort_values())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
imp.plot(kind="barh", color="steelblue", ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Top 10 Features (Random Forest)")
ax.set_xlabel("Importance")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Alcohol consumption typically rises to the top, which is unsurprising since drinking habits track closely with smoking, alongside personality and lifestyle measures.

## Takeaway

Lifestyle and personality carry a real but imperfect signal about smoking. The models distinguish current smokers from never-smokers with about 66% accuracy and an AUC near 0.72, well above chance but far from certain. Notably, the flexible random forest barely edges out simple logistic regression, a useful reminder that a more complex model is not automatically better. This page demonstrates the full binary-classification workflow on messy, mixed-type survey data: a column-transformer pipeline for preprocessing, stratified train/test splitting, class balancing, and threshold-independent evaluation with ROC-AUC.
